title: IBM Spyre AI Accelerator Card (75W PCIe Card with 128GB of LPDDR5)
content:
Introduction to IBM Spyre Accelerator
The Spyre AI Card, also known as the IBM® Spyre Accelerator, is a high-performance, energy-efficient PCIe add-on designed to enhance AI inferencing capabilities on IBM Z® and LinuxONE systems.
For more information, see the content solution for Spyre Accelerator for IBM Z and LinuxONE available at https://www.ibm.com/support/z-content-solutions/spyre-accelerator-z-and-linuxone/.
Key features include:
- Architecture & Specs
  - Equipped with 32 AI accelerator cores, capable of handling matrix operations and low‑precision workloads for high throughput.
  - Manufactured using Samsung’s advanced 5 nm process node.
  - Each card supports up to 128 GB of LPDDR5 memory, with ensembles of up to eight cards delivering 1 TB memory and massive AI performance.
  - Delivers exceptional AI compute—exceeding 300 TOPS per card—while consuming just 75 W.
- Usage & Benefits
  - Delivers advanced ensemble AI workflows by complementing the on‑chip Telum‑II AI accelerator, enabling multi‑model inferencing for tasks like real‑time fraud detection and code assistance.
  - Enables on‑premises generative AI use cases—such as running Watsonx Code Assistant™—while maintaining the inherent security, reliability, and data locality of the IBM Z environment.
Appliance Control Center for IBM Z & IBM LinuxONE
The Appliance Control Center (ACC) is a secure application for deploying software appliances on IBM Z and IBM LinuxONE systems. It integrates with the Hardware Management Console (HMC) to manage and monitor appliances across multiple systems. ACC enables users to upload SSC-based appliances and updates, then handles their installation. By streamlining deployment, control, and maintenance, ACC simplifies appliance lifecycle management.
Spyre Support Appliance for IBM Z & IBM LinuxONE
The Spyre Support Appliance (SSA) is a dedicated solution for managing, monitoring, and diagnosing Spyre cards attached to IBM Z Logical Partitions (LPARs). SSA continuously tracks all connected Spyre cards to optimize performance and enable proactive error handling. Upon initialization, it activates all assigned Spyre cards and performs real-time monitoring—checking every second for newly added or removed cards, and dynamically handling initialization or cleanup. Beyond lifecycle management, SSA collects key metrics and health data to maintain performance and support early issue detection.

report.summary: IBM’s Spyre PCIe card brings 128GB LPDDR5 and over 300 TOPS of AI inference to IBM Z and LinuxONE at just 75W per card.
report.background: Enterprise AI inference is moving closer to transactional data as regulated industries seek generative AI without sending sensitive records to the cloud. IBM Z and LinuxONE already host mission-critical workloads and include on-chip Telum-II AI acceleration, but complex multi-model inference needs more capacity. IBM’s Spyre add-in card extends those systems with dedicated off-chip AI compute, high memory bandwidth and low power draw. Built on Samsung’s 5nm process, it reflects a broader industry shift toward inference-specific, memory-rich accelerators that fit existing data-center power and security envelopes rather than relying solely on power-hungry GPUs.
key_points: Spyre packs 32 AI accelerator cores, Samsung 5nm manufacturing, up to 128GB of LPDDR5 per card, more than 300 TOPS, and a 75W power envelope. IBM says ensembles of up to eight cards can reach 1TB of memory and massive inference throughput.

The card complements Telum-II, IBM Z’s on-chip AI accelerator, to support ensemble and multi-model inference. IBM positions it for real-time fraud detection, code assistance and other latency-sensitive workloads that combine several models in one transaction flow.

Spyre enables on-premises generative AI on IBM Z and LinuxONE, including Watsonx Code Assistant, while preserving data locality, security and reliability. That matters for banks, insurers and governments that cannot easily move sensitive code or transaction data to public clouds.

IBM provides Appliance Control Center to deploy software appliances through the Hardware Management Console, and the Spyre Support Appliance to initialize, monitor and diagnose Spyre cards attached to logical partitions. SSA checks for card changes every second and collects health metrics.

Spyre is not a general-purpose GPU replacement. It targets IBM Z and LinuxONE transactional AI inference, where high memory per watt and tight integration with enterprise security and management matter more than broad CUDA-style developer ecosystems.
report.impact: Spyre signals further diversification of AI inference hardware beyond GPUs, especially for memory-heavy, low-power and data-local enterprise workloads. For the AI industry, it validates inference-specific accelerators tied to mainframe and LinuxONE transaction systems, where security and reliability outweigh raw training performance. Developers targeting IBM Z will gain a new inference target alongside Telum-II, but they must learn LPAR, ACC and SSA workflows and accept a narrower software ecosystem than CUDA. Regular users may see benefits indirectly: faster fraud checks, local code assistance and generative AI features that keep sensitive data inside enterprise systems rather than sending it to cloud APIs.
report.tools: Watch IBM watsonx Code Assistant, IBM Z and LinuxONE documentation, and the Appliance Control Center and Spyre Support Appliance for deployment and monitoring. IBM’s Z content solutions page is the best starting point. No public open-source Spyre SDK appears in the source, so developers should monitor IBM LinuxONE trial programs and watsonx tooling rather than expect a CUDA-style community stack.
